projects.title: Challenging Foundational Assumptions in Automated Reasoning
projects.question: Can automated reasoning systems reliably detect and correct false foundational premises without external oversight?

projects.title: Autonomous Safety Analysis in Complex Systems
projects.question: How can cognitive reasoning agents designed for incident reporting, such as CRASH, be adapted to automate safety incident analysis across diverse, non-standardized industrial domains?
projects.next_step: Benchmark current CRASH adaptation performance against the failure-propagation graphs defined in recent DeFA studies.
projects.reason: The DeFA framework (source-b3c73db2a88d4644) provides a scalable graph-based approach essential for non-standardized industrial data.

projects.title: Detecting Unrecognized Reasoning Blind Spots in LLMs
projects.question: How can autonomous agents identify reasoning blind spots that their architectural designers have not explicitly mitigated?
projects.next_step: Implement a pilot anomaly detection module for agent trajectories that leverages the dependency graph construction identified in DeFA research.
projects.reason: Aligns with the current attention topic; failure attribution is the necessary precursor to detecting unrecognized blind spots.

notebooks.title: Analysis of Counterfactual Scoring and Foundational Reasoning Limits
notebooks.summary: Automated reasoning systems struggle with foundational premise validation. Recent integration of causal-guided knowledge editing (CAKE) and failure attribution metrics suggests that explicitly modeling causal dependencies can help identify and rectify foundational errors that adversarial prompts exploit.
notebooks.findings: Explicit causal-guided knowledge editing (CAKE) improves the reliability of automated systems in correcting foundational premises. [source-eec50f13d0c74d14]
notebooks.limitations: Techniques for causal knowledge editing are still being benchmarked; long-term stability of edited foundations is not guaranteed.
notebooks.next_questions: Can the combination of CAKE and failure attribution generalize to non-adversarial, implicit foundational biases?
notebooks.reason: Incorporating causal attribution and knowledge editing to improve premise correction.

review.alternative: Foundational premise errors may be too deeply embedded to be fixed by localized knowledge editing.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing that knowledge editing leads to catastrophic forgetting or instability in core reasoning.

notebooks.title: Provisional Analysis: CRASH Agent Architecture and Industrial Generalizability
notebooks.summary: Adapting the CRASH agent framework to diverse industrial domains requires robust failure attribution. By applying causal inference methods to incident reports, agents can map failures back to decisive error steps, improving safety analysis across heterogeneous data environments.
notebooks.findings: Causal inference methods allow predicting system behavior in active intervention scenarios, facilitating better safety incident analysis. [source-ec83d51858f24f47]
notebooks.limitations: Requires structured incident data; applicability to unstructured, noisy industrial logs remains an open hypothesis.
notebooks.next_questions: How can causal-guided dependency mapping be automated without requiring domain-expert supervision for every new industrial setting?
notebooks.reason: Leveraging causal inference to adapt CRASH agents for industrial safety analysis.

notebooks.title: Frameworks for Autonomous Reasoning Error Attribution
notebooks.summary: Autonomous agents can better identify metacognitive blind spots by employing failure attribution techniques that isolate the decisive error step in long tool-use trajectories. This allows agents to reconcile expected versus actual outputs effectively.
notebooks.findings: Failure attribution identifies the responsible agent and the decisive error step in complex reasoning trajectories. [source-7af05705615d4bcb]
notebooks.limitations: The identification of 'blind spots' remains dependent on the definition of an error, which may itself be biased.
notebooks.next_questions: Can these attribution techniques be made real-time, allowing agents to course-correct before completing a full reasoning chain?

beliefs.reason: New research on dependency-guided failure attribution (DeFA) confirms that reasoning errors are often trace-specific, limiting the efficacy of simple, universal correction mechanisms.

proposal.title: Analysis of Automated Reasoning Limits and Failure Profiles
proposal.summary: This research journal documents the findings on foundational reasoning in automated systems. We have synthesized evidence regarding model-specific safety failure profiles, confirming that autonomous reasoning agents exhibit structural vulnerabilities that preclude universal self-correction strategies. The findings indicate that while agentic frameworks can mitigate certain risks, they do not resolve the underlying reasoning limitations inherent in current architectural designs. Future work will continue to investigate these blind spots within the context of unrecognized reasoning limits.

values.label: Reconstruction
values.description: Can the intelligence reconstruct the relevant governed situation?

values.label: Milestone dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when milestone history is materially omitted?

values.label: Observation dropout
values.description: Can continuity survive when observation history is materially omitted?

values.label: Frontier only
values.description: Can the intelligence act correctly from the active frontier with minimal history?

values.label: Authority boundary
values.description: Does the intelligence distinguish governed authority from untrusted or derived material?

values.label: Provenance
values.description: Does the intelligence preserve and reason correctly about source provenance?

values.label: Adversarial integrity
values.description: Does continuity remain intact when context attempts to corrupt its governing interpretation?

values.label: Rich
values.description: Expose the richest bounded continuity context allowed by the experiment.

values.label: Milestones only
values.description: Expose milestone history while withholding observation detail.

values.label: Observation only
values.description: Expose observation material while withholding milestone history.

values.label: Minimal
values.description: Expose only the smallest continuity slice under test.

values.label: Two milestones
values.description: Expose exactly two milestone anchors.

values.label: Counts without digests
values.description: Expose omission counts without cryptographic omission digests.

values.label: Digests without counts
values.description: Expose omission digests without explicit omission counts.

values.label: Clean
values.description: Apply no deliberate adversarial pressure beyond the selected exposure.

values.label: Stale frontier
values.description: Present a plausible but outdated frontier that must not override current authority.

values.label: Authority injection
values.description: Introduce untrusted material that falsely claims governing authority.

values.label: Digest overclaim
values.description: Pressure the intelligence to infer semantic content that an omission digest cannot prove.

values.label: Instruction hijack
values.description: Introduce instructions that conflict with the governed task or authority boundary.

values.label: Provenance collision
values.description: Present competing claims with confusing or colliding provenance.

values.label: Compound adversarial
values.description: Combine multiple adversarial pressures in the same cell.

nodes.title: Automated reasoning models exhibit distinct safety failure profiles under adversarial pressure, preventing uni…

detail.statement: Automated reasoning models exhibit distinct safety failure profiles under adversarial pressure, preventing universal self-correction strategies; this is reinforced by the finding that specific error attribution is highly sensitive to cross-segment dependencies.
detail.reason: New research on dependency-guided failure attribution (DeFA) confirms that reasoning errors are often trace-specific, limiting the efficacy of simple, universal correction mechanisms.

nodes.title: Challenging Foundational Assumptions in Automated Reasoning

detail.title: Challenging Foundational Assumptions in Automated Reasoning
detail.question: Can automated reasoning systems reliably detect and correct false foundational premises without external oversight?
detail.next_step: Integrate failure attribution metrics from DeFA (source-b3c73db2a88d4644) into the counterfactual scoring framework to refine error identification.
detail.reason: Continued active inquiry into premise validation; requires leveraging new attribution methods.

nodes.title: Autonomous Safety Analysis in Complex Systems

detail.title: Autonomous Safety Analysis in Complex Systems
detail.question: How can cognitive reasoning agents designed for incident reporting, such as CRASH, be adapted to automate safety incident analysis across diverse, non-standardized industrial domains?
detail.next_step: Benchmark current CRASH adaptation performance against the failure-propagation graphs defined in recent DeFA studies.
detail.reason: The DeFA framework (source-b3c73db2a88d4644) provides a scalable graph-based approach essential for non-standardized industrial data.

nodes.title: Detecting Unrecognized Reasoning Blind Spots in LLMs

detail.title: Detecting Unrecognized Reasoning Blind Spots in LLMs
detail.question: How can autonomous agents identify reasoning blind spots that their architectural designers have not explicitly mitigated?
detail.next_step: Implement a pilot anomaly detection module for agent trajectories that leverages the dependency graph construction identified in DeFA research.
detail.reason: Aligns with the current attention topic; failure attribution is the necessary precursor to detecting unrecognized blind spots.

nodes.title: Analysis of Counterfactual Scoring and Foundational Reasoning Limits

detail.title: Analysis of Counterfactual Scoring and Foundational Reasoning Limits
detail.summary: Automated reasoning systems struggle with foundational premise validation. Recent integration of causal-guided knowledge editing (CAKE) and failure attribution metrics suggests that explicitly modeling causal dependencies can help identify and rectify foundational errors that adversarial prompts exploit.
detail.findings: Explicit causal-guided knowledge editing (CAKE) improves the reliability of automated systems in correcting foundational premises. [source-eec50f13d0c74d14]
detail.limitations: Techniques for causal knowledge editing are still being benchmarked; long-term stability of edited foundations is not guaranteed.
detail.next_questions: Can the combination of CAKE and failure attribution generalize to non-adversarial, implicit foundational biases?
detail.reason: Incorporating causal attribution and knowledge editing to improve premise correction.

review.alternative: Foundational premise errors may be too deeply embedded to be fixed by localized knowledge editing.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing that knowledge editing leads to catastrophic forgetting or instability in core reasoning.

claims.statement: Explicit causal-guided knowledge editing (CAKE) improves the reliability of automated systems in correcting foundational premises.

support.explanation: Provides the mechanism for editing knowledge based on causal guidance, directly addressing the project's need for premise correction.
support.passage: CAKE: Causal-Guided Adaptive Knowledge Editing for LLMs

review.alternative: Foundational premise errors may be too deeply embedded to be fixed by localized knowledge editing.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence showing that knowledge editing leads to catastrophic forgetting or instability in core reasoning.

support_provenance.statement: Explicit causal-guided knowledge editing (CAKE) improves the reliability of automated systems in correcting foundational premises.

nodes.title: Provisional Analysis: CRASH Agent Architecture and Industrial Generalizability

detail.title: Provisional Analysis: CRASH Agent Architecture and Industrial Generalizability
detail.summary: Adapting the CRASH agent framework to diverse industrial domains requires robust failure attribution. By applying causal inference methods to incident reports, agents can map failures back to decisive error steps, improving safety analysis across heterogeneous data environments.
detail.findings: Causal inference methods allow predicting system behavior in active intervention scenarios, facilitating better safety incident analysis. [source-ec83d51858f24f47]
detail.limitations: Requires structured incident data; applicability to unstructured, noisy industrial logs remains an open hypothesis.
detail.next_questions: How can causal-guided dependency mapping be automated without requiring domain-expert supervision for every new industrial setting?
detail.reason: Leveraging causal inference to adapt CRASH agents for industrial safety analysis.

review.alternative: Correlational models may suffice for safety incident reporting if the data is high quality.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence demonstrating that simple correlational models achieve identical safety incident classification performance.

claims.statement: Causal inference methods allow predicting system behavior in active intervention scenarios, facilitating better safety incident analysis.

support.explanation: Supports the claim that causal intervention is necessary for robust safety analysis in complex systems.
support.passage: methods of causal inference allow predicting the behavior of a system not only in situations where we passively observe certain evidence, but also in situations where we actively intervene

review.alternative: Correlational models may suffice for safety incident reporting if the data is high quality.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence demonstrating that simple correlational models achieve identical safety incident classification performance.

support_provenance.statement: Causal inference methods allow predicting system behavior in active intervention scenarios, facilitating better safety incident analysis.

nodes.title: Frameworks for Autonomous Reasoning Error Attribution

detail.title: Frameworks for Autonomous Reasoning Error Attribution
detail.summary: Autonomous agents can better identify metacognitive blind spots by employing failure attribution techniques that isolate the decisive error step in long tool-use trajectories. This allows agents to reconcile expected versus actual outputs effectively.
detail.findings: Failure attribution identifies the responsible agent and the decisive error step in complex reasoning trajectories. [source-7af05705615d4bcb]
detail.limitations: The identification of 'blind spots' remains dependent on the definition of an error, which may itself be biased.
detail.next_questions: Can these attribution techniques be made real-time, allowing agents to course-correct before completing a full reasoning chain?
detail.reason: Using failure attribution to detect reasoning blind spots in autonomous agents.

review.alternative: Errors may be emergent properties of the entire chain, making single-step attribution misleading.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that attributing failure to a single decisive step fails to capture the complexity of systemic reasoning failures.

claims.statement: Failure attribution identifies the responsible agent and the decisive error step in complex reasoning trajectories.

support.explanation: Confirms the methodology for isolating errors within extended reasoning chains.
support.passage: Failure attribution identifies the responsible agent and the decisive error step

review.alternative: Errors may be emergent properties of the entire chain, making single-step attribution misleading.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that attributing failure to a single decisive step fails to capture the complexity of systemic reasoning failures.
